name: Cortisone injections for keloids

lead: A clinician injects a corticosteroid, usually triamcinolone, directly into a keloid to flatten it and ease itching, aiming for a flatter, softer scar.

The steroid is described as reducing inflammation and fibroblast activity in the scar. Wikipedia lists it among standard keloid options, introduced in the mid-1960s, and current registered trials compare it with fluorouracil, metformin, lasers and botulinum toxin.

paras: It is given in repeated clinic visits over time and is sometimes combined with 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser in adults. Keloids often follow piercings, especially of the earlobes, and are most common between ages 10 and 20.

It is a prescription procedure done by clinicians. A published case report describes a reaction after an injection of triamcinolone with lidocaine, and systematic adverse-event data were not in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: A clinician injects steroid, often triamcinolone, into a raised keloid to reduce inflammation and fibroblast activity so the scar flattens and softens. It is a long-standing option now being compared with newer agents in small trials.

lead: Intralesional corticosteroid injection, commonly with triamcinolone acetonide, is a treatment in which a corticosteroid is injected directly into a keloid, a raised scar that grows beyond the original wound. Wikipedia reports that intralesional corticosteroids were introduced in the mid-1960s and are said to reduce fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching [1].

Keloids are most common in people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latin American ancestry, often appear between ages 10 and 20, and frequently follow piercing, particularly of the earlobes [1]. Wikipedia describes corticosteroid injection as one of several options, sometimes combined with 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser in adults [1].

Registered clinical trials continue to compare steroid injection with other agents, including 5-fluorouracil, metformin, botulinum toxin and laser-assisted delivery. A published case report documents a reaction after an injection of triamcinolone with lidocaine [2].

paras: Steroid injections are used to flatten and soften keloids and reduce itching. Wikipedia lists them alongside surgery, radiation, cryotherapy, pressure therapy and silicone sheeting, noting that surgical excision alone has a recurrence rate of 70 to 100 percent and that combining it with other therapies lowers recurrence [1]. Steroid injection after excision is itself studied, as covered in the keloid surgery and radiation entry.

A 2001 French case report described a patient who experienced fear of dying after an intra-keloid injection of triamcinolone acetonide with lidocaine, a reaction labelled Hoigne's syndrome [2]. The sources reviewed do not provide systematic adverse-event rates.

Registered trials include intralesional treatment of keloids in a 45-person phase 3 study that began in December 2024 and is recruiting [3]; triamcinolone versus triamcinolone with fluorouracil after surgery (7 participants, completed) [4]; intralesional metformin versus triamcinolone (30 participants, phase 2, completed) [5]; steroid injection alone versus combined with Nd:YAG or erbium laser (20 participants, completed) [6]; fractional ablation-assisted triamcinolone delivery (25 participants) [7]; and botulinum toxin to prevent recurrence (28 participants, phase 4, completed) [8]. Registry records reviewed list no outcomes, so effect sizes are not given here.
Keloids occur in discussions of piercing and scar care. No forum material was available for this entry, so community claims are not documented.

timeline.event: Intralesional corticosteroid injections are introduced for keloids. [1]
